teaser: America's most patriotic picture was painted in Germany, to cheer up defeated revolutionaries.
review_notes:
Leutze's intention to encourage German liberals after the failed 1848 revolutions: standard reading, check wording.
First version damaged by studio fire in 1850, later in the Kunsthalle Bremen, destroyed in an air raid in 1942: check.
More than 50,000 visitors in New York in 1851; bought by Marshall O. Roberts for $10,000: check.
Worthington Whittredge posing for Washington and the steersman: check.
Identifications of the crew (James Monroe holding the flag, Black oarsman sometimes called Prince Whipple, Scottish bonnet, possible Native American steersman, rower in red sometimes read as a woman) are traditional, not documented by Leutze.
Stars and Stripes adopted June 1777; crossing on the night of December 25 to 26, 1776.
Smaller version sold at Christie's in 2022 for about $45 million: check.
Dimensions 378.5 x 647.7 cm.

lesson.text: In 1849 Emanuel Leutze was on the losing side. The revolutions that had swept the German states the year before, demanding constitutions and a united nation, had been crushed. In Düsseldorf, where he lived, friends were discouraged, silenced or packing for exile.

Leutze answered with a painting about another cause that had once looked finished. In December 1776 the American rebels were beaten, freezing and deserting. On the night of December 25, George Washington led them across the icy Delaware River to surprise the enemy at Trenton. It worked, and the war turned.
This is a picture about not giving up, painted for Europeans who had just lost. The American subject was the example: a revolution at its lowest point, one night before it recovered.
Leutze was German and American at once. Born in 1816 in Schwäbisch Gmünd, he grew up in Philadelphia, then returned to Germany in 1841 to study painting and stayed for almost twenty years.

The canvas is enormous: about 3.8 meters high and 6.5 meters wide (12 by 21 feet). The figures in the boat are life-size. With that much surface, Leutze needed a strong skeleton so the scene would read in one glance from across a hall.
Three lines hold this huge scene together.

lines.label: The pyramid
lines.text: Boat, bodies and flag pile up into a triangle, with the flag at the summit. A pyramid is the most stable shape a painter can use: this crew will not tip over.

lines.label: The pole
lines.text: At the bow, a long pole shoves the ice away. Its diagonal points up and forward, the direction of the whole boat.

lines.label: The gaze
lines.text: Washington looks ahead toward the far shore and the pale sky. Nobody else in the boat has time to look that far.

lesson.text: Notice what that pyramid is made of: thirteen colonies' worth of very different people squeezed into one small boat. Leutze could not know who actually rowed that night. He chose his crew as a portrait of a nation, each one a type his viewers would recognize.

lesson.title: Who is in the boat
lesson.text: Move from the bow to the stern and meet four of the twelve.

spots.title: A Scottish bonnet
spots.text: The young rower leaning over the side wears a flat Scottish cap, a nod to the many recent immigrants in the army.

spots.title: The Black oarsman
spots.text: Beside him rows a man of African descent, often said to represent Prince Whipple. Black soldiers and sailors did serve in Washington's army.

spots.title: The flag bearer
spots.text: The officer gripping the flag is traditionally identified as Lieutenant James Monroe, who fought at Trenton and later became the fifth president.

spots.title: The steersman
spots.text: At the stern, a man in a fur cap, fringed leggings and an embroidered pouch guides the boat. He is usually read as a frontiersman, or as a Native American.

lesson.text: Farmers in broad hats, a man with a bandaged head, a rower in red whom some viewers take for a woman: the list goes on. They disagree about clothes and probably about everything else. In the boat, they pull the same way.

Leutze had no American soldiers at hand in Düsseldorf, so he recruited American art students and tourists as models. The painter Worthington Whittredge posed in a copy of Washington's uniform, and for the steersman too.

Historians have had fun with the mistakes. The real crossing happened in the dark, in sleet. The boats were larger, heavy cargo boats with high sides. Standing like that would have been a fine way to fall in. And then there is the flag.

The Stars and Stripes above Monroe's head was only adopted in June 1777, six months after the crossing. Leutze knew he was painting a legend, not a report. He even added a small sign in the sky that this long night is ending.
One last star is still shining before daybreak. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The morning star
spots.text: A single bright star hangs in the clearing sky at upper left, directly in the path of Washington's gaze. It announces dawn, and with it a change of fortune.

lesson.text: The painting itself nearly did not survive its own birth. In 1850 a fire broke out in Leutze's studio and damaged the first canvas. He started again at once on a second one, the picture you are looking at, and shipped it to New York in 1851.
The repaired first version ended up in the museum of Bremen, Germany. It was destroyed there in 1942 by a British air raid, a strange end for a picture about a war against Britain.

In New York the response was huge. More than 50,000 people came to see it within months, and a collector, Marshall O. Roberts, paid $10,000 for it. Engravings carried the image into parlors and schoolrooms across the country. It entered the Metropolitan Museum in 1897.

spots.title: Washington
spots.text: He stands with one knee forward, cloak lined in red, sword at his side. His profile is cut out sharply against the brightest part of the sky.

spots.title: The flag
spots.text: The wind wraps it into heavy folds. You can make out stars on the blue field: a flag that did not yet exist on that night.

spots.title: Horses and cannon crews
spots.text: Behind the main boat, others carry rearing horses and more soldiers. The army had to bring its artillery and animals across too.

spots.title: The ice
spots.text: Thick slabs of ice crowd the foreground, painted with green shadows and glassy edges. They make the cold almost physical.

spots.title: The bandaged man
spots.text: A soldier clutches his hat against the wind. A cloth is wrapped around his head, a reminder that this army was already wounded and exhausted.

spots.title: The rower in red
spots.text: Long hair, a soft face, a red jacket: this figure is sometimes read as a woman in men's clothing. Leutze left no explanation.

lesson.text: The image never stopped traveling. It has been quoted in cartoons, advertisements and protest art, and it appears on the New Jersey state quarter. In 2022 a smaller version painted by Leutze sold at auction for about $45 million. The German exiles it was meant to comfort are mostly forgotten. Their picture is not.

quiz.question: Which defeat pushed Leutze to paint this subject?
quiz.explanation: He wanted to encourage discouraged European liberals with an American example.

quiz.question: What is historically wrong with the flag?
options: It was adopted only in 1777, after the crossing
It was a British flag that night
quiz.explanation: The Stars and Stripes dates from June 1777, six months later.

quiz.question: Who is the flag bearer traditionally said to be?
quiz.explanation: Monroe fought at Trenton and later became the fifth president.

quiz.question: What happened to the first version of the painting?
options: It hangs in the White House
It was destroyed in Bremen in 1942
It was cut into pieces and sold
quiz.explanation: Damaged by a studio fire in 1850, it was later destroyed by an air raid.

quiz.question: Which shape organizes the boat and its crew?
options: A pyramid with the flag at the top
quiz.explanation: Bodies and flag build a stable triangle.

quiz.question: Who posed for Washington in Düsseldorf?
quiz.explanation: Leutze used American students and visitors as models.

facts.text: The painting was made in Germany.
facts.explanation: Leutze painted it in Düsseldorf and shipped it to New York in 1851.

facts.text: The real crossing took place in bright morning light.
facts.explanation: It happened at night, in sleet; the dawn light is Leutze's invention.

facts.text: The figures in the main boat are about life-size.
facts.explanation: The canvas measures roughly 3.8 by 6.5 meters.
